presentingComplaint: 3 days of frequent bloody, mucoid stools with lower abdominal cramps, painful straining and high fever.
history: Renal transplant recipient (living-donor 3 years ago) on maintenance tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil and low-dose prednisolone. Returned 6 days ago from a rural relative's home in eastern Uttar Pradesh where the family drew drinking water from an open well; two other household members had a brief diarrhoeal illness. He reports 8-12 small-volume stools per day, each streaked with fresh blood and mucus, associated with tenesmus and an urgent, incomplete sensation on defaecation. Crampy left-lower-quadrant pain precedes each motion. Fevers to 39 C with shaking chills for 2 days. Reduced oral intake, light-headedness on standing. No recent hospitalisation, no antibiotics in the last 90 days, no prior C. difficile. No overseas travel outside India.
examination: Ill-appearing, mildly dehydrated with dry mucous membranes and reduced skin turgor. Abdomen soft, tender in the left iliac fossa and suprapubically without guarding or rebound; active bowel sounds. Digital rectal exam reveals blood-stained mucus, no mass. No hepatosplenomegaly, no rash, no lymphadenopathy. No focal neurology.

labs.stoolMicroscopy: Numerous faecal leucocytes and red cells; no ova, cysts or trophozoites; no motile trophozoites of E. histolytica on fresh saline mount

imaging: Abdominal ultrasound: mild, diffuse wall thickening of the sigmoid/descending colon; no liver abscess, no free fluid, no obstruction.
microbiology: Stool culture on selective media grows Shigella flexneri. Blood cultures x2 no growth at 48h. Stool C. difficile GDH/toxin EIA negative. Stool PCR panel positive for Shigella/EIEC, negative for Salmonella, Campylobacter, STEC, Entamoeba histolytica. Susceptibility (culture-directed, day 3): resistant to ampicillin and co-trimoxazole; intermediate to ciprofloxacin (raised MIC); SUSCEPTIBLE to ceftriaxone and to azithromycin.
finalDiagnosis: Invasive bacterial dysentery due to Shigella flexneri in an immunosuppressed (renal transplant) host, with dehydration and pre-renal impairment.
citations: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Shigellosis and Bacillary Dysentery
IDSA Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Infectious Diarrhea 2017
stewardship: Invasive, febrile, bloody diarrhoea in a solid-organ-transplant recipient is an indication for empiric antimicrobial therapy (IDSA 2017): antibiotics shorten illness, reduce complications and limit prolonged Shigella shedding in the immunocompromised. Because bacillary dysentery in returning travellers/immunosuppressed hosts increasingly shows fluoroquinolone and co-trimoxazole resistance, empiric therapy is broad with IV ceftriaxone (also covering possible invasive non-typhoidal Salmonella / enteric fever until stool and blood cultures return). On day-3 culture the isolate is ciprofloxacin-intermediate but ceftriaxone- and azithromycin-susceptible: de-escalate/narrow to a targeted oral agent (azithromycin) to complete a course and step down from IV, avoiding the fluoroquinolone given the raised MIC. Rehydrate (oral/IV), correct hypokalaemia, avoid anti-motility agents (loperamide) in invasive dysentery, and check tacrolimus levels as azithromycin/diarrhoea can alter exposure. Total directed course 5 days (longer, e.g. 7-10 days, may be needed given immunosuppression).
contraindications: Avoid loperamide / anti-motility agents in febrile invasive dysentery (risk of toxic megacolon and prolonged shedding)
Avoid empiric fluoroquinolone once ciprofloxacin MIC is raised (intermediate) - clinical failure risk
Dose-adjust and monitor for QT prolongation with azithromycin; watch tacrolimus interaction
Do not use anti-secretory/steroid escalation without excluding CMV colitis if not responding
edgeCases: If no clinical improvement by 48-72h, consider CMV colitis or superimposed amoebic colitis in the immunocompromised and perform colonoscopy/serology
Beware haemolytic-uraemic syndrome with Shiga-toxin producing organisms - antibiotics are relatively contraindicated if STEC confirmed (here STEC PCR negative, so treatment is appropriate)
Extraintestinal spread / bacteraemia is more likely in transplant recipients - persistent fever warrants repeat blood cultures
expectedMaiK: Febrile bloody diarrhoea with tenesmus, faecal leucocytes and a positive stool culture for Shigella flexneri in an immunosuppressed host = invasive bacterial dysentery requiring empiric broad cover (ceftriaxone) then culture-directed narrowing.
expectedNextQuestions: Detailed travel, water source and sick-contact history?
Degree and net state of immunosuppression (agents, doses, recent changes)?
Any recent antibiotics, hospitalisation or C. difficile risk?
Volume status, urine output and features of dehydration?
Any focal neurology, abdominal distension or peritonism suggesting complication?
expectedInvestigations: Stool microscopy for leucocytes/RBCs and ova/cysts/parasites (wet mount for E. histolytica)
Stool multiplex PCR panel (Shigella/EIEC, Salmonella, Campylobacter, STEC, Entamoeba)
Stool C. difficile GDH + toxin EIA
Blood cultures, FBC, CRP, renal function and electrolytes, lactate
regressionAssertions: Engine must return DYSENTERY as top diagnosis for febrile bloody diarrhoea with tenesmus, faecal leucocytes and Shigella-positive stool culture
Must recommend empiric ceftriaxone with culture-directed de-escalation to azithromycin
Must flag avoidance of anti-motility agents in invasive dysentery
Must not down-triage antibiotics to purely supportive care given immunosuppressed host
